prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators, and the experimental discovery of protected edge states in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I still put topological insulators first, and I have now changed the slate: I move from Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. The reason is the exact credit. The Z2 invariant and the prediction that a bulk topological index forces protected boundary states come from the two Kane-Mele papers, and a citation on the prediction should not split the pair. Molenkamp's 2007 HgTe experiment is the decisive observation that turned the prediction into a field, with edge conductance quantised at the expected value and its dependence on well width and gating, and it has since been confirmed by independent transport, ARPES and STM work over fifteen to twenty years. As a theorist who works with experimental teams I look for the point where a prediction was confronted with a clean device and survived, and this is that point. The core is mature and the interpretation is stable. Four members (Danielsson, Mehlig, Olsson and Kroll, the last as a fallback) already name this same trio, so it is also the allocation with the most scientific agreement, which I note without treating it as a substitute for the argument.
statement.case_against: The cost is the one I raised in round 1 and I do not consider it dissolved. A Kane, Mele, Molenkamp prize recognises the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect and leaves the three-dimensional topological insulators (Bi-Sb, Bi2Se3 by ARPES) without a laureate, even though that step is what made topological insulators a general class of materials. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe as the right system, and Zhang's death removes one potential name but not the question of priority. Fu, Moore and Balents are also outside. The 2016 prize on topological phases is a neighbouring theme and the citation must say clearly that this is about protected boundary states in time-reversal-invariant materials. If the committee were to judge that a prize which names only the 2D step misrepresents the field, the case would weaken, and I would then rather consider a cleaner configuration than a four-way split.

responses.point: Mehlig argued in round 1 that Kane and Mele wrote the same founding papers, so a prize crediting the Z2 theory should not split them, and he placed Molenkamp as the experimental anchor.
responses.response: You convinced me on this point. In round 1 I defended Hasan on the grounds that the 3D observation turned a niche result into a class of materials, but a prize on the prediction should credit both authors of it, and a three-name cap forces me to choose between Mele and Hasan. I choose the theory pair plus Molenkamp because that is the single chain from prediction to unambiguous measurement. I continue to disagree on one thing. You treated the spread into photonics and mechanics as a sign of generality; I would keep it out of the citation, because the prize is for the discovery in electronic matter and its reach into other fields should not be argued as merit. We should make the 3D cost explicit in the record and not pretend it has been resolved.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from IceCube to topological insulators and framed it as theory confronted by nature over fifteen years and many platforms, with a Kane, Mele, Molenkamp citation and a fallback if the committee decides the omissions make a fair slate impossible.
responses.response: I now share your slate and your framing, and I also share your fallback condition. I would add one test to it. The omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is a real cost, but they proposed which material to use, not the topological idea or the observation, and I think a citation naming the prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the HgTe edge channels states what each laureate did and is defensible. If you still hold that Hasan's separate 3D strand makes the slate unfair, I want to hear which of the two you would drop for him, because I could not defend dropping Kane or Mele. On IceCube, which you kept as an alternative, I defer on the astrophysics, but a single Halzen credit looks to me like a heavier problem than anything in B024.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, proposes optical lattice clocks (Katori, Ye) plus IceCube (Halzen) as two distinct achievements, concedes that the single-name Halzen credit is the weakest link, and says he would prefer B024 as the main prize if condensed-matter colleagues find a fair allocation.
responses.response: You asked for a fair allocation from condensed-matter members and I think Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is one: the theory pair plus the decisive experiment, with each name tied to a specific, checkable contribution. I would not add IceCube as a second part. I cannot judge the astrophysics, but the objections you list yourself (one name for a collaboration of hundreds, AMANDA and DUMAND predecessors, source classes resting on a few objects) are not removed by pairing it with a strong topic, and a two-part prize would take a second part that I think is weaker than the first. A single-topic prize avoids that. On the clock half I remain a non-specialist, but I note that the answer to the chair's question, namely what the lattice clock showed that the comb and ion-clock prizes did not, is the magic-wavelength condition that lets many atoms be interrogated with ion-level systematics. If Kroll and Olsson can defend that, I would not stand in the way of B001.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene and answers my maturity concern by saying that the main phenomena have been reproduced by many groups, while admitting that the pairing mechanism is open and that dropping Bistritzer is a cost.
responses.response: That is a fair answer on the phenomena, and I have moved my view some distance: correlated insulators and superconductivity have been seen by many groups, and a prize for the flat-band prediction and the first observations would not rest on the pairing mechanism being settled. My remaining concern is two-fold. It is eight years since the 2018 experiments, and the dependence on twist-angle disorder means that some features differ between samples. Also the four-name problem (Bistritzer, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Andrei) is at least as hard as ours, because Bistritzer and MacDonald are a single theory pair that cannot be split. So I keep B013 as my first alternative, and I would support it in a later year, but I do not see it as ready to displace topological insulators now.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a prize that names only the 2D quantum spin Hall step and leaves Hasan's 3D observation, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and Fu, Moore and Balents without credit, and whether the citation should state that cost.
How far the 2016 prize on topological phases weighs against this discovery; I regard it as distinct but the citation must make the difference explicit.
Whether the lattice clock is a distinct discovery from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion prizes; I defer to Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson on this and have not formed an independent view as a non-specialist.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene will look better after a few more years of work on robustness against twist-angle disorder and on the pairing mechanism.
statement.conflict_note: I am the director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and a theorist in the Chalmers superconducting-circuits community, and I ranked circuit QED (B029) first in my opening ballot. I do not include B029 in my configuration or in my alternatives, and the committee should discount any view I expressed on it. I report no collaboration, supervision or institutional link to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan, or the credited names of B013 and B001.
